INCREASES IN TAXATION ON GASOLINE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Since the last election there have been no less than 12 increases in the price of gasoline, despite the Liberal party's rather empty commitments to the people of Canada. In view of the fact that Canadians are now contributing a total of 56 cents to federal coffers on every gallon of gas consumed, or 33.7 per cent of the $1.66 per gallon now being charged in Ontario, and because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) misled this House yesterday by stating that the federal government received only 10 per cent from petroleum revenues, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis):
That this House instruct the Prime Minister to tell the whole truth about energy revenues, and further that the government be instructed to redirect these excessive tax revenues into a much needed energy tax rebate program for low and middle-income families.

When a home owner is forced to give up his or her house because he or she cannot afford the mortgage payments, CMHC simply takes over the house and sells it. That the government provide an intelligent explanation for the lack of assistance to the 500,000 Canadians renewing their mortgages this year if they can afford the Liberal interest rates.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Since record high interest rates are having a devastating effect on home owners, and on small business generally, and since many operators of small group homes which provide invaluable community support services to the disabled and handicapped, senior citizens, disturbed children, adolescents and others, are finding it virtually impossible to continue with this work because they do not have the funds at their disposal to meet the interest rates being demanded on renewed mortgages, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House instruct the Minister of Finance to re-examine the government's interest rate policy, and that he immediately bring forward legislation that will place a moratorium on all mortgage foreclosures and bankruptcies on group homes until interest rates are returned to an acceptable and humane level.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member misunderstands almost completely the nature of the increased charges which were brought before the House by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The hon. member knows that there is a blended pricing system in operation in Canada by which the Government of Canada is averaging the price of domestic and imported oil in order to maintain a lower general price for the Canadian consumer. He knows that in order to operate that particular pricing regime it is necessary for the treasury of Canada to subsidize the importation of oil. He knows that perfectly well.
All that was done by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was to ensure that these increased costs, for example, occasioned by the production cutbacks by the province of Alberta, would not be reflected in an increased deficit but would maintain the fiscal plan put forward in the budget, namely, that about $360 million would be assigned to this import subsidy program in the current fiscal year.
If we fail to take the action which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources took, then of course we would be doing what the hon. member for St. John's West is always asking us not to do, namely, add to the deficit. Minutes have been taken only in the past few decades. It is a procedure followed by cabinet forms of government. The secrecy of discussions between ministers and the frankness of discussions are essential to the very notion and existence of cabinet government.
There was, to my knowledge, one exception, when minutes were shown to a royal commission. It occurred when Commissioner McDonald suggested there might be some reasonable and probable cause to believe that maybe some infringement of the law had taken place. In that instance our government consented to show the McDonald commission that particular minute.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, last evening when we adjourned debate on Bill C-57,1 accepted the invitation of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) to comment on the proposed taxes as they affect the Canadian wine industry. This invitation was also extended by my good friend, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who is celebrating his twenty-fourth anniversary today as a member of the House of Commons and, I might say, a very valuable member.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
As one who has spoken out on innumerable occasions in the House and across the country on the wine industry, my feeling at this moment is one of relief in terms of the taxes proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen). Although no one welcomes taxes, even those imposed upon such traditional areas as wine, spirits, beer and tobacco, my relief stems from my ability to compare the proposals of the Minister of Finance and those of the former minister of finance who invited me to participate.
The plea of the hon. member for St. John's West last night for the workers in the beer and wine industry was strange. It was a very eloquent plea, I might add. One would be hard-pressed to come to the conclusion that he was referring to the same people in the wine and beer industries against which he brought in some Draconian measures.
What were the two main features of the Crosbie budget? I suppose insensitivity was the main one. There was an excise tax on gasoline of 18 cents and, in some cases, 25 cents. I am thinking of the farmers of Lincoln, fruit farmers, grape growers and farmers in general. Also I am thinking of fishermen and the effect of this tax on the transportation of handicapped people. When one couples the tax on the wine industry specifically with the proposals included in the Tory budget, one can understand the anger, frustration and disappointment of the grape growers and fruit farmers of the Niagara peninsula.
Excise Tax

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: You are misleading the House, do not forget the rebate.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance is proposing that once a year the tax on wine, beer and spirits be indexed to the cost of living in such a manner that the relationship between the tax and the retail price will be constant. This is nothing unusual. It is precisely the philosophy of the ad valorem tax. It is the reverse of the indexing which is part of our tax system when incomes are calculated for tax purposes and when the cost of living index is used to increase the guaranteed income supplement every three months.
I should like to return to the proposals of the hon. member for St. John's West and why I am relieved our Minister of Finance had an open mind and was sympathetic to the representations which I and others made to him. More important, he agreed that it would be wrong to implement the recommendations of his predecessor, the hon. member for St. John's West.
What did the former minister propose to do? He is the same person who rose last night to castigate my party, particularly myself and others, for not caring about the wine industry. What did he propose in his 1979 budget which defeated the Tory government just in time to give the country a second chance?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: Tell the whole story.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
The "hon. chorus" has begun already and I have hardly started. Traditionally the wine and beer industry has been considered an extension of the agricultural sector. The hon. member opposite knows that. After all, corn, wheat, grapes, rye, apples and barley are all important to those industries. Without those industries, there is no outlet or very little outlet for our grapes. Thus, it is in the interests of everyone to foster and encourage the growth of those industries.
Thanks to the enlightened approach to the whole problem of the grape growing industry of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in recent years, there has been a transitional period during which some grape growers have been able to convert to different types of vines, fruit and grapes. This has permitted the Canadian industry a greater latitude. Now they are able to produce table wines similar to German wines. This takes time, approximately five, six or seven years.
The former minister of finance decided that wine and beer would no longer be considered an extension of the agricultural industry. He decided that it was to be another source of income. He was totally insensitive to the representations of the farmers of Lincoln and the Niagara Peninsula. It was efficient and effective; it was drawn up by faithful public servants in his department. The basis of the tax on wine and beer henceforth was not to be related to the fact that they were an extension of the agricultural industry; it was to be linked to alcoholic content. These public servants recognized that there are variations in the alcoholic content of wine. So in order to receive every cent in taxation, or to tax it to its ultimate, they

June 10, 1981
Excise Tax
categorized wine. They put into one category what is known as fortified wine with an alcoholic content of over 14 per cent.
Of course, the danger was obvious. The grapes which are traditionally used for that category of wine are grown in the Niagara Peninsula. They are known as the Labrusca grapes. To come along and impose a Draconian tax-and I will mention the figures in a few minutes-on that industry, at a time when Canadian tastes were changing from fortified wines with high alcoholic content to table wines, was the straw which broke the camel's back.
This is a serious point; I am not trying to make political hay. Canadians had an opportunity to assess the Crosbie budget and to put that party out of office. I am sure they would do it all over again, because the last election was fought on the commitment of the Conservative party to reintroduce precisely the same budget with all its flaws which I am pointing out.
The impact of the Crosbie budget, as opposed to the budget of the present Minister of Finance, would have been to increase the tax on wines with over a 14 per cent alcoholic content by $2.45. But the budget proposal of the minister of finance of the Conservative government was to raise the excise rate on wine in which the alcoholic content was over 14 per cent from 55 cents to $3, an increase of $2.45-a percentage increase of 445 per cent.
The ex-minister spoke eloquently last night about the beer industry. He said that the workers of Canada traditionally love their beer. He spoke eloquently about their ability to export their product. But how did he treat them when he had the opportunity to put into practice his concerns for the same people? We are talking today about a matter which occurred less than two years ago. He was prepared to raise the excise tax on beer by 29 per cent, which again would have a detrimental effect on the farmers of Canada. At the same time he was limiting the tax on alcoholic spirits to 5 per cent-a 90-cent increase from $16.25 to $17.15.
It is obvious that the ex-minister, who was castigating civil servants last night, was quite prepared to accept their insensitive advice, which was to base taxes on alcoholic content, thereby showing no concern, no recognition or appreciation of the fact that the beer industry and the wine industry of this country are extensions of the agricultural community. He did not recognize that an expanding wine industry is important to the agricultural growers in the Niagara Peninsula, if you do not want them to give up in despair and hand their properties over to developers, or allow cities such as St. Catharines to expand and become more urban than rural.

speechtext:
We won't get into that, because my chance will come. You guys were very happy about what you did to me in Air Canada! I can talk about that another day, about the jackals surrounding a wolf.
The point I want to talk about is the impact the proposals of the former minister of finance would have had if the present Minister of Finance had adopted them. For all intents and purposes, if we were voting on the proposals tonight, and they passed, then the possibility of the grape growers continuing in business would be limited. A 300 per cent tax on fortified wine at the very time when there was a movement away from heavy wines would have a devastating effect. It would be the end of the industry. That was the proposal of the ex-minister of finance who last night was indignant because the present minister has suggested that once a year we increase tax according to a formula simply to maintain the real value of that tax, which has fallen significantly over the last ten years.
I am aware of the time, Mr. Speaker. I realize my allotted time is almost up. I would love to go on and talk about the other impacts the ex-minister's budget proposals would have had on the wine industry. I would like to deal with the excise tax on gasoline, something which we said we would never impose and which we have not imposed. That tax, coupled with the tax on wine, caused real concern in the industry. We voiced that concern to the present Minister of Finance. We met daily, weekly in caucus and in private meetings, with farm groups, with the wine institute and with the marketing board. We pleaded with the minister and his officials, telling them that such a tax proposed by the ex-minister of finance, and adopted for a short period of time by the present minister, was not only detrimental but discriminatory to the wine industry and the beer industry.
What was the result of our representations? I have been teased in this House by members opposite-and I should not blow my cool, it is not normal for me-for having made representations at every opportunity, which is why I was called upon last night to participate in this debate. I am glad that I am recognized in this House as the voice of the wine industry. I am pleased that I represent that industry so well and so effectively, the 900 farm families who are involved in the wine industry. I am pleased and proud that I have made that impact on the member for St. John's West. I am pleased that I have had enough influence with the present Minister of Finance and his very able colleague, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres).
In conclusion, I want to point out what we succeeded in doing. We succeeded in having the Minister of Finance depart from that insensitive policy of his predecessor, to restore the traditional relationship between wine, beer and alcohol and to introduce a nominal tax which was more than accepted with good grace by the wine community of this country. If indexing proves to be a problem, I am sure the Minister of Finance will have no hesitation to rescind that policy after he has had an opportunity to test it.

Hon. members of this House have a responsibility to safeguard the welfare of the public. As best we can, regardless what side of the House we may come from, we must preserve the revenues of our constituencies. We should be concerned about the fact that every time we reach into a taxpayer's pocket, be it a corporation or an individual, we are depriving that taxpayer of an opportunity to use those funds for the purpose of expanding business operations or for necessary expenditures, from the standpoint of consumer spending. That should be our prime purpose.
Historically, Parliament has, indeed, been a place which has preserved and protected the citizenry against the rapacious appetites of government. As the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) honestly disclosed in the House, we know that ministers of finance have been led around by the nose by their deputy ministers and others in the bureaucracy seeking endless ways to dip into the public purse and into the pockets of the citizens of the country. We should be on our guard to protect the public from the appetite of government.
This particular measure has a built-in inflationary advantage. An ad valorem tax will produce either more revenue or less revenue for the treasury, depending upon the price of the item. There has not been a minister of finance known to man who has ever desired to collect less taxes. Therefore, it must be assumed that when a finance minister imposes an ad valorem tax, he intends to get more and not less. Since the tax is raised as a direct consequence of the fixing of the price of the item, we must know that the government expects the price of commodities to increase. If the government telegraphs to the public in Canada that it expects that the price of every item which is subject to tax under this bill will increase, then, in order that the public may, in fact, maintain a level of income which is equivalent to the level of increases in prices, the public should expect that the price of public services and the price of the public's disposition of commodities should increase.
By this measure, the government is therefore inducing the public to expect inflation to continue. It is asking the public to increase the price of goods and services. It is inviting the public to disregard the pleas of the government for restraint and to follow its lead in psychologically anticipating inflationary growth.
We have heard a great deal about the comparison between this measure and one which may have been contained in the budget of December, 1979.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say only a few words on this particular amendment, primarily to clarify some of the misstatements and misunderstandings which have been put forward by the hon. members opposite.
This particular provision indexes a fixed dollar amount tax, which converts it to exactly the same form as the retail sales tax that has been with us for years, the manufacturers' excise tax or value added taxes or ad valorem taxes. It does not in any way, shape or form allow the federal government to increase the real value of the tax that has been received. Indeed, it does just the opposite; it prevents the erosion of the tax base so that the real value of the tax received stays the same. It prevents the situation where every several years the government must recapture lost ground with a new tax.
As the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble) indicated, provincial governments have seen fit to do exactly the same thing and it makes a great deal of sense. Once a logical taxation structure is established for a certain commodity, in this case alcohol and tobacco, then it remains in place. We do not want to alter it and then, at a later date, bring in new legislation to modify it. By taking the steps we have, we ensure that the structure stays the same; the real value of the tax stays the same. It does not increase over time and it does not add real value to the tax base of the federal government, as it has not done to the tax base of provincial governments in the case of the retail sales tax or manufacturers' excise tax.
When talking about a bill as serious as C-57, it is unfortunate that hon. members opposite cannot keep to fair and honest debate regarding the facts, the merits and demerits of the case, instead of creating illusions for the public and accusing the government of motivations that do not exist or of doing things which are not in the public interest. That is not true, Mr. Speaker. The facts are there, the explanation is simple and I have tried to provide it to hon. members.

Who are the financial advisers, the tax experts, the economists who claim that this is the correct approach for the government to use in collecting additional revenue? On whose behalf do they speak when suggesting the concept of indexing as set out in this bill? The concept of indexing is insidious in that it puts Canadian consumers at the mercy of foreign exchange differences. As inflation increases in a particular country and the value of that currency relative to ours changes, that fact may have a significant effect on the consumer price subgroup on which this particular index will be based.
If the cost of hops was to increase significantly in one year because of crop failures or the introduction of new equipment or machinery to the industry, for example-and I identify hops as one of the components of the particular consumer index subgroup-that would mean that the price of wines would also increase, the price of tobacco would increase and the price of distilled spirits would increase in this country. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as we are concerned, this set of motions incorporates some very important principles. While the motions themselves articulate wording required to alter some of the principles presented in this particular bill, I want to comment first on the general nature of what is incorporated in each of the motions we are debating.
Because closure is upon us, it appears we will not have an opportunity to discuss in the necessary depth all of the assembled motions the Speaker has considered. I suppose in that respect one would want to keep one's comments relatively short so that at least we can have an opportunity to deal as best we are able with all the various motions and have some deliberation in the House on the problems associated with the position of the government.
When we are talking about the small newspapers in Canada, including independent weeklies, community newspapers, the ethnic press and so forth, we are talking about something which touches the very soul of Canada and about a reflection of the real views, attitudes, aspirations and concerns of Canadian citizens. I do not suppose there are many in this House who feel that some of the major newspaper chains really reflect the concerns of the regions, various municipalities, small villages and rural areas of Canada in any real way. Because the major newspaper chains are in fact chains, they reflect only the policies of those corporate entities.
What we are concerned about here are the voices of Canadian citizens. I suppose our free speech is threatened today in a number of ways. The opportunity for individual Canadians, groups and communities to speak out is being hampered. The government should be going a long way to preserving that independent voice for Canadian citizens and communities.
One of the countries I have had an opportunity to study at some length in terms of newspapers is Sweden. Here is a country that a number of years ago found there was general acceptance among all parties that the ability of individual citizens to speak out was being limited and hampered. So the government took it upon itself to introduce a number of measures which encouraged the small weekly, biweekly, triweekly newspapers, the various ethnic papers and trade journals and so on. They felt it was important that each individual citizen, agency and organization had before it a vehicle whereby its point of view and concerns could be expressed in a clear and articulate way.
The government of Sweden saw that this ability was being eroded, that in fact the growing concentration in the newspaper industry was making it more difficult for individuals to speak out, was making it more difficult for the various regions to be reflected in the media, particularly the newspaper media. So they took a number of steps to encourage the introduction of new and small newspapers. They were prepared to give a certain amount of government advertising to the smallest of newspapers, quite contrary to this government's policy where in fact its advertising goes through their media agencies to the large metropolitan dailies, essentially laundered through the national newspaper chains. However, Sweden took a different approach. They felt it was in their vested interests, as a government reflecting the views of its citizens, to ensure that the small independent newspapers were not only revitalized, but that those already in existence were preserved.
What we see there, Mr. Speaker, in this collection of motions is an attempt by the government essentially to undermine the small newspapers of Canada. I do not think for a moment that is a result of some devious mind across the way making an attempt to reduce the number of small independent voices across this country. But I suspect, like so many other aspects of this bill, a bureaucratic oversight, a notion that some bureaucrat in the finance area had which would result in more revenue accruing to the government, without thinking through the social consequences. It is, if you like, beyond the mind set or the terms of reference of the advisers within the finance committee.
Well, I might say, Mr. Speaker, that we have gone to some lengths to determine what this particular bill will do to the small newspapers of Canada. Quite frankly, I doubt if there is a member of this House who has not been approached by newspapermen from within their own ridings, small newspaper publishers and printers concerned about what this measure is going to do to their ability to continue in operation, particularly to continue competing with the large national newspaper chains. They are hanging on with some difficulty, and I know that in my own riding of Kamloops-Shuswap I made a point of approaching each of the weekly and biweekly newspapers to ask how this particular legislation was going to influence them. I must say there were not many pleased publishers in my particular riding and beyond, that I contacted. They see this again as one more hurdle to be overcome to enable them to compete in this extremely competitive area, particularly when the competition is unequal. It is difficult for a small newspaper in Clearwater, British Columbia, to compete with the large metropolitan dailies flooding into the area every day. But it is important that the people of that community have the opportunity to voice their concerns over their community's welfare through letters to the editor in their own independent newspaper.
This is a bill that is going to levy a tax on newspaper inserts. Now, we feel that it is important that the consumer is made well aware of price changes, of opportunities that entre-
June 10, 1981

preneurs take to provide a product at lesser cost to the consumer. We feel that the more informed people can be in our communities, particularly during these times, the better it is. Here is a situation where a firm decides to take out a page in a newspaper and advertise a commodity and there will be no tax on that; but if it decides to enclose an insert in that newspaper with perhaps a different colour to make it more attractive, it will be paying a tax on that. We on this side of the House feel that somehow that is not just, that it is not treating everyone equally, and it is encouraging people to reduce perhaps the amount of advertising they do which is going to reflect directly on the income of the small newspaper and their cash flow.
We are also very concerned about the government's decision to attempt to redefine what is a newspaper, to suggest there has to be a certain percentage of editorial comment or news and a certain percentage of advertising. We feel that is something that should be left to the independent newspapers to determine for themselves. If they feel for some weeks it is just as well to go with 90 per cent advertising and 10 per cent news and editorial comment, that would be fine. Other weeks it may perhaps be 50-50. But I think it is very important that we recognize that that decision should be made at the local level, not here in Ottawa by this particular piece of legislation. Let us do what we can to encourage the newspapers of Canada, especially the small, independent community newspapers which reflect the differences in view of the citizens and regions of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, there are many amendments dealing with newspaper advertising, one from the minister which shows that instead of 75 per cent, the figure has now become 80 per cent. Well, that makes little difference because what we are concerned with here is a matter of principle, of determining what is a newspaper by the amount of advertising. There are a number of categories in the act.
Now, the section as it originally reads refers to college and school annuals, magazines and literary papers, unbound, regularly issued at stated intervals, not less frequently than four times yearly; newspapers, sheet music, materials used exclusively in the manufacture thereof. What has been done here is to blow up that word "newspapers".
As far as the act is concerned, the sections at pages 35, 36 and 37, there is a great deal to do. We did hear extensive representations.
I am quite staggered by the utter silence of members from the province of Quebec who told me at the outset that they were impressed by the representations of Quebec weekly newspapers. When looking at the list of Quebec newspapers that have made representations, especially the weeklies in all the rural ridings, I wonder why all hon. members are not in the House trying to block this bill, because we all received the

same representations, from the regional weeklies, Metropolitan Weeklies Ltd., the Select Newspapers of Quebec, the Quebe-cor group, the South Shore weeklies, M ichael Publishing I ncor-porated and Suburban Newspapers.
When they appeared before us, and here I am referring to Issue No. 46 of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for Thursday, March 26, at page 6, Mr. Jean-Paul Cloutier was acting as spokesman for the majority of newspaper owners who made their representations on that day. I want to quote what he said:
Mr. Chairman, I would now like to outline the contents of this particular intervention. If we have made so many presentations concerning Bill C-57, it is because to us it is extremely important. In our opinion, it is the first time that the government, through tax legislation, has gone so far to affect directly our sector, the regional newspapers. We are affected directly by the law in two ways. First, any advertising which is over 75 per cent of the newspaper content-
Let us say in passing that we will change that to 80 per cent.
-is taxable at a rate of 9 per cent. Secondly, the bill provides for a 9 per cent tax on all advertising supplements or inserts in newspapers. Those are the two main features of the bill which affect us somewhat. Mr. Chairman, this morning we would like to tell you how this affects us and offer a few suggestions. We have already made some suggestions. Before the Senate committee particularlyOn that point I would ask the minister to tell us what the Senate committee had to say about that. The senators also made their recommendation, but the Liberal senators were in a majority and I do know that the report did not endorse the measure proposed by the Minister of Finance.
We have realized from the minister's presentation that he does not intend or wish to tax newspapers.
No, he does not want to tax newspapers. However, he wants to eliminate certain abuses, or so he says, so he grabs his sledgehammer to crush a bug. It is very simple. By striking, by using that kind of formula, he is trying to eliminate certain abuses. There may very well be some, but it is not by taxing or by forcing the newspapers, particularly the small weeklies, to measure every inch of their columns on a monthly, or a single, or a quarterly basis.
Mr. Cloutier goes on to say:
Also, in our conversations with politicians and officials, we have noted that the aim of the bill was to correct a certain abuse. However, we cannot agree with the means that the minister and the government have taken in order to reach these objectives, since it affects us quite directly. We are quite aware of, Mr. Chairman, how difficult it is for the government to intervene in the media sector, particularly the written press. We know how touchy is public opinion in this respect, it is evident in that governments, both at the federal and provincial levels, have created commissions of enquiry. The Kent commission is a case in point since it is now receiving briefs and holding hearings. We, indeed, presented a brief to the Kent commission, in which we mention Bill C-57 and the problems it would create for the weekly newspapers. I think the Kent commission is now well aware of this problem.
So as we can see, the culprits are not weeklies from the rural areas and small towns or even the small dailies with a modest circulation; yet this will cost a pretty penny. So, they will have to measure because that is what it is based on; 80 per cent of the newspaper content can be advertising. If it is a little over,

bang! The newspaper is taxed. Especially if they include inserts which are not catalogues but advertising supplements prepared by firms like Beaver Lumber, Canadian Tire, Radio Shack and even the large department stores like The Bay, Simpsons-Sears, Eaton and Woodward out west, and many others that include those inserts in the newspapers. That is the way they distribute theirs, and it is certainly the best way.
The post office is not very reliable and in rural communities and small towns, newspapers enjoy the best distribution system. So if this service is provided to the public, then why-1 do not know what is considered improper in this matter, what rubs the minister the wrong way. Is it because these are the same type of flyers that are distributed in shopping centres? Is that the problem? What is the problem? What is improper? It seems that we have to tax and to determine what is a newspaper. The papers said that they were newspapers, period.
They have been called newspapers, unless the advertising content shall exceed a certain amount over a stated period. Then they are no longer newspapers within the true meaning of the term, and they are subject to this special tax on the entire publication.
It is very easy for the big city metropolitan daily, which runs 140 pages to 150 pages in perhaps a couple of editions per week, to have the base from which to spread their excesses from day to day. If they come up to 79.9 per cent over a four-month period, they will be within the law; but they will be able to get away with a great deal more than the small newspapers. I am surprised by the absolute silence- [Translation]
-the stubborn silence of the Quebec members. I remember quite well that when the committee was dealing with that point they were incensed. Were they putting on an act for the benefit of the Quebec organizations' representatives? You could see them beating their wings. That is what they were doing. But when the time comes now to make representations or state openly that the proposed legislation is unfair, they are mute. What sort of people are they? Have they been ordered to keep their trap shut? That is not what they said when their constituents were here. No, sir! They were certainly going to speak up and make strong representations! Representations? Do we hear any? Not a word! You should have heard what they said to the people, in committee and outside the House, but now that the time has come for them to stand up in the House and be counted, it is quite a different story! What is more, they are speechless. They cannot utter a word. How are they going to explain that back home? Could the hon. lady tell us how she is going to get away with it? Personally, I always speak through the Chair. The parliamentary secretary should be the last one to make gestures and try to teach me a lesson.
Mr. Speaker, I still wonder how they are going to explain the situation. Were these newspapers abusing the law? In what way? And if they were not abusing the law, why are they threatened with a 9 per cent tax, as provided under this bill? Precisely. The hon. member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi), who is sitting next to the minister-that is quite surprising; we must have a word with the representatives who appeared before the committee. Have a word with Mr. Cloutier. Have you had a word with Mr. Cloutier? Have you had a word with Mr. Cyrenne and the others who were there? We are going to say: we oppose at this time the implementation of these provisions as worded. The minister can indicate exactly what abuses had to be corrected. Then we will be able to determine, as I said earlier, whether he used a sledgehammer to kill a bug or, in a different context, a gun powerful enough to kill an elephant to shoot a mere mouse. That is why I support the motion moved by my colleague the hon. member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). I hope, in turn, that they will support our amendments, and there are a whole lot of them. Some will ask, why 80 per cent, why not 90 or 99.9 per cent? Because, naturally, there comes a time when one must draw the line, and that line is set at some percentage or other. Some may claim that to be arbitrary. When a decision is to be made, one has to assume the responsibility for whatever judgment has been made. A first decision was made setting a certain percentage; then, as a result of the representations made by the industry and hon. members, the Minister of Finance adjusted his decision to take into account the representations made to him. I think that publishers of weeklies now recognize that this gives them sufficient latitude.
The other point is advertising. The member for Edmonton West explained very well why advertising inserts should be taxed. He stated that in such cases, weeklies are only a distribution network. Now if we consider the argument, it should be acknowledged that there is some consistency in that tax levy. I am rather surprised to note how we have been expressing our social concern over the past few days especially with regards to taxation in Canada. The minister has said that he cannot understand how it is that members of our party are becoming worked up about taxes on alcohol. I will say to the minister that the social philosophy is quite simple. I think we expressed it at some length yesterday with respect to the indexation of taxes on beer, wine and distilled spirits. The fundamental principle, first of all, is that we do not want to see the cost of living and the cost of pleasure of the average Canadian go up without any form of control. In our view, the policies of the federal government are at least partly responsible for the inflationary situation in which we are at the present time. We do not want to see the government becoming the beneficiary of that very inflation.
With respect to the inflation principle, I think the minister is perhaps a little abstract, if not fuzzy-headed, if he is unable to see the philosophy-not a word that I use too often-or the basis of our concerns.
With respect to the amendments which have been put forward today by my colleague, the hon. member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), and with respect to the similar amendments which have been put forward by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who is in the Conservative party, I will say to the minister that I think there is a very clear difference between his approach to this problem and ours. The government's approach to this problem is one, if you like, of Cartesian rationality with respect to proposals which come to it. It says, "Ah ha! There is a problem here", when someone has brought to its attention an inequity in the tax system, which tax system is just chock full of absurdities, anomalies and inequities. The government moves back and forth in trying to slap a tax on here, or slap a tax on there. The minister's department has created more loopholes and anomalies than we will ever be able to talk about or discuss in the

June 10, 1981
Excise Tax
time which has been so kindly and gracefully allocated to us over the next day and one-half by the government.
However, I do want to say to the minister that our approach is to look at what is really happening in the country and in the communities of this country; it is not to look out from the fifteenth floor of the Bell Canada building down on Elgin Street to determine, from some kind of abstract rational assessment, what the answer to this particular problem will be. Our approach is to see what is actually happening in the community newspapers and in the human economy of this country represented by people in all parts of this House. We will ask what the effect of that tax will be on the lives of those communities. The minister might say that we are just special pleaders and are only pleading for whatever interest comes before this House. I will use the exact words of the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) when he said that in a good many of the amendments which we are putting forward we are just trying to feather the nest of some particular interest group which has come before us.
I want to tell the minister that we have been very particular. We have responded not simply to whatever pressure group has happened to put on an effective lobby, but to what we have actually seen happening in communities.
This last Easter I happened to be visiting the south shore of Nova Scotia where I was doing some politicking and some resting. I happened to go into the offices of a community newspaper in the town of Liverpool. This newspaper is owned by one individual. It is not part of any kind of chain, it is not part of some multinational enterprise, nor is it a part of an association of chains in one province or one region of Canada. It is a newspaper which is owned locally and which services an entire area. It provides community news for the entire community of Liverpool and the surrounding area.
As I walked in to say hello to the publisher of that newspaper, the very first questions he asked me were, "What is going on with the excise tax, and what is going on with the taxation of our advertising? Why is the government picking on us?" We went through his costs, we went through his problems, we went through the cost of material which has gone up, we went through the whole range of problems which that newspaper was facing. We looked at what the potential effect would be if the government, willy-nilly, decided to go after all insert and supplementary advertising and taxed them as they have never been taxed in North America since the time of the Stamp Act in the 70s.

I want to say to the minister that it is when one talks to people in this kind of a situation that the policies of the government make no sense because the definitions are, by their
very nature, arbitrary. When it is 75 per cent, people start complaining and want to make it 80 per cent. One could just as well have said 85 per cent, 95 per cent, 50 per cent or 25 per cent. There is no law that the minister has been following; it is just a rule chosen by a civil servant after pressure here or a knuckle here from a minister, saying, "We are getting a lot of heat on 75. Could you put it up to 80?"
What we have attempted to do with our amendments, and what the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap has attempted to do with our amendments, is to say, "All right. There is a problem." There is a problem, because many of the large commercial chains have used the circulation of newspapers as a cover for the distribution of their catalogues in order to avoid the excise tax that falls on all commercial advertising done outside the context of the newspaper.
We have defined catalogues, Mr. Speaker. We do not think that our definition is necessarily the source of all truth but we think that it is at least an attempt to make this point clear. If the minister is concerned with dealing with an abuse, he should do so and not offer legislation that will have a detrimental effect on the cost, the integrity and, indeed, the very life of hundreds of community newspapers in the country.
The government has never learned the importance of following the politics of experience rather than simply the politics of abstract rationality. If it looked at the politics of experience, which is what our social philosophy is about, and if it looked at the effect of this legislation on the viability of the community newspaper, it would learn something. I see the minister shaking his head. Mr. Speaker, I have never seen a study of the community in newspaper industry issued by the Department of Finance which would indicate what the effect of this will be on that industry. We have not been provided with any indication of the effect that this will have on their revenues or on the behaviour of advertisers. The government needs to consider the policies of experience, the politics of fact, the politics of looking at what the actual effect will be.
Yesterday the government was prepared to say that beer and wine have just as deleterious an effect on the health of the consumer as have distilled spirits. Mr. Speaker, one's normal experience does not usually show that a glass of scotch has the same effect on someone as a glass of beer. The experience of the average consumer would show that to be nonsense. The same thing applies to the experience, not of the powerful lobbies or of those seeking to avoid any kind of taxation-and I agree with the minister that we have to be firm when dealing with those people-but to the experience of institutions and people and the effect this legislation could have on them.
The minister asks what our social philosophy is based on. Mr. Speaker, it is based on experience, on what the life of these communities is and on the importance of recognizing the contribution that these newspapers make to the life of a community, and not simply to the profitability of a chain or the growth of a monopoly. The communities are important to
June 10, 1981

us and I am sure the maintenance of life in the community is what has driven many of us into public life.
In effect, the government says "If you are opposed to this tax, then you have to show us why we should not impose it." That is the burden that the minister puts on us. It shows how far this government has gone when it says that we, somehow, have to prove to it why a tax should not be imposed. It has the wrong notion of where the burden lies. If the government wants to change the system of taxation on community newspapers, if it wants to establish a definition of what is a newspaper and what is not, if it wants to tax all supplements produced for two or more newspapers, then it has an obligation to tell us why it wants to do this and the precise effect it will have on the economy and the life of community newspapers.
It is incredible that the minister should suggest to the House that every time that the government imposes a tax, those opposed to it or affected by it have to give the government an explanation of why it should not be imposed.
I should like hon. members opposite to suggest that in the next election campaign. I should like to see them put in their leaflets, "Vote Liberal and tell us why you should not be taxed". I wonder how far the average Canadian would let them go on a platform like that, yet that is the attitude the Liberal government brings to this House.
The reason we are opposed to this particular suggestion is that the definition of a newspaper is arbitrary.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
This is a serious subject and one which has received extensive and comprehensive coverage. Certainly anyone who has a newspaper or a weekly newspaper published in his riding, has been a recipient of lobbies and representations. I use the word lobby in the good sense. Personally I do not think there is anything wrong with that kind of representation. Surely having the opportunity to hear from people who are knowledgeable in the field gives us an opportunity to learn. How we sort it out and how we apply it is something we have to bring to the House to discuss.
In my riding, I have a Thomson newspaper, the Sarnia Observer, which is a daily newspaper. Also there is an independent weekly paper called the Sarnia Gazette. Representatives from both papers made representations to me on this subject. As a result of that, I did a fair amount of studying of the subject matter to determine whether what was being suggested in this legislation was unfair and whether changes should be made or, for that matter, if the provision in this bill should be dropped altogether.
I was surprised to find-maybe I should not have been surprised-that no other advertising appearing in newspapers is in fact taxed. In other words, if a person places an ad in a newspaper, the person is not taxed for that ad. What we have in dispute, however, is not the advertising in the newspaper but the inserts. If an insert goes into a newspaper, whether it is published by that newspaper or whether it is published elsewhere and brought to the newspaper for distribution, that insert at the present time is not taxed.
In endeavouring to get all the information we could bring before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, we had no fewer than three groups from the newspaper industry making representations, the Hebdos from the province of Quebec, the daily newspaper association and the weekly newspaper association outside of Quebec. Having

June 10, 1981
Excise Tax
heard all of their representations and having heard the representation of the publisher of the Sarnia Observer, I wanted to determine if what is taking place in this particular instance would be unfair, particularly to weekly papers, and particularly to the smaller papers. It has been my experience in dealing with the larger industries, be they newspapers, petrochemical companies or whatever, that they can usually cope with increases or deal with issues as they see them because they do have, as the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood mentioned, the expertise of the lawyers or the know-how to either get around the problem or to find a way to at least lessen the impact of a particular tax.
When you look at the provision as it is presently constituted, it says that if more than 90 per cent of the space in any single issue of a newspaper is devoted to advertising, it is going to be subject to the tax. I point out, it says more than 90 per cent. It seems to me that any newspaper worth being called by that name will have no difficulty with that particular section.
Looking at the second part-and in this connection the minister's department has moved an amendment-we find that it says that all issues of a newspaper in any calendar quarter will be subject to the tax if more than 75 per cent-that is going to be changed to 80 per cent-of the space per issue in more than 50 per cent of the issues of the newspaper in that calendar quarter is devoted to advertising.
Here again, I do not see that as having a significant impact or causing difficulty for the legitimate newspapers to cope with. It will prevent people who would like to be classified as newspapers but are really nothing more than advertising circulars from abusing the regulation. In other words, people who are trying to classify themselves as newspapers and are not will be subject to this tax.
I have mentioned to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) that I intend to watch what impact this will have. I will be following it up with my local daily and with local newspapers to determine whether this tax will have a detrimental impact on them, not only from the standpoint of business, as mentioned by the previous speaker, but also as to how they put their newspapers together.
It has been suggested to me by the publisher of the Sarnia Observer that these changes will have an impact on the way he puts his newspaper together, for instance, what he puts on the front page or how much editorial content he can have. When I read these clauses, however, I am not sure that the point has been made. I am prepared to listen, however. Nor will I let this subject drop if I see that it is having the kind of impact which the publisher of the Sarnia Observer suggests. The publisher of the Observer wrote to me on May 1, 1981. In part, his letter reads:
To say I am quite upset over this would be an understatement, as I feel the effects of this will be a definite threat to the continuing financial success of this newspaper.
That is a bit of hyperbole. I do not think the Sarnia Observer, which serves an area of some 150,000 people and is a member of the Thomson newspaper chain, will be put out of
business or will suffer that significantly. What does concern me is how he feels, and I shall quote again from his letter as follows:
How Mr. MacEachen can say that the tax on inserts is not an interference or infringement on the freedom of the press is beyond me.
What he is suggesting is that these taxes will dictate to him the manner in which he will have to put his newspaper together. Personally I do not see that at this time, given the 90 per cent figure and given the 80 per cent figure per issue in more than 50 per cent of the issues, how it will have that kind of impact.
One of the greater disappointments to me as chairman of the finance committee was the representation made by the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association by Mr. O'Callaghan, I believe with some reputation with the Edmonton Journal. During a committee hearing when questioning Mr. O'Callaghan to find out what his real feelings were on the subject, we asked him whether, if he had a four-page weekly, which is not an unusual thing with newspapers that are starting out, and a Sears catalogue of some 200 pages placed in that four-page weekly, he would still consider that part of the newspaper? Mr. O'Callaghan answered yes. He then wondered why members of the committee were aghast that he would make that kind of representation. Surely if you are making a representation to a committee, you should be honest enough to make a presentation so that members can have some kind of a dialogue. That was an area that concerned me because Mr. O'Callaghan who was representing the daily newspapers association, did not seem to be prepared to compromise. He made the point that he was responsible as a newspaper publisher for what was contained in the ads in the catalogue and, therefore, that was "part of the newspaper". I could not buy that argument.
Another area of concern to me came about as a result of a circular sent out by the Department of National Revenue, and it concerns interpretation. It seems to me, and I think the point was in part being made by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood, that some other newspapers will be able to get around this definition of an insert. It will not be an insert. Instead, the document will be preprinted and those inserts will contain some editorial comments or comments about travel, perhaps a description of the local community, as well as some editorial comment or newspaper comment. It will be open to them not to call that an insert. They will use numbered pages so that it will look as though it were part of the newspaper. Larger newspapers will be able to do that. I am not so sure that the weeklies will because most of them, I suspect, do not print the matter in their own shops. It is something brought in by the kinds of groups which the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was suggesting. Therefore, they will not be in a position to number pages or to put anything on those pages which comes from Canadian Tire or whatever is brought to them. If that works to the disadvantage of the weeklies, it is something we should be looking out for.
As the bill is now drafted, with the amendment from the 75 per cent to the 80 per cent, I do not think it will have the dire
June 10, 1981

consequences suggested to me by the publisher of the Sarnia Observer. It will probably make him a little more conscious of the amount of editorial content that goes into his newspaper. But given these large figures of 90 per cent and 80 per cent, I do not see a restriction being put on him in the way he puts his newspaper together. After he has seen the legislation and heard the debate in the House maybe he will be prepared to agree that it will not have the detrimental effect he suggests.
At one time newspapers had no advertising in them whatsoever. They relied solely on the charge for the newspaper. Moving away from that, and in the interest of supporting newspapers, advertising was allowed to be put into a newspaper without any tax. I do not think anybody objected to that. Some of these inserts now going into the newspapers are a further evolution of the advertising being done in that newspaper. We all agree with Mr. O'Callaghan that some of the inserts might contain editorial comment, and the publisher and editor of that newspaper might very well be held responsible for it.
If this is one more evolution of advertising in the newspaper, maybe we will need to look at this. The Minister of Finance indicated that he is going to bring down a budget in the fall-I believe he said October. If that is the case, this may be another area he will have to look at to see if it is having a detrimental effect or if changes should be made so we do not prevent what I might call legitimate inserts from appearing. I have not defined them by moving an amendment to this clause. If this is something that will hurt newspapers and put weeklies out of business and concentrate newspapers in the hands of too few people, it deserves a second look.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate today should indicate to the government that this tax is not necessary, that it will interfere with freedom of the press and will put a number of newspapers out of business. The minister said he had to choose a figure; 75, 80, 85 or 90 per cent. Why did he have to choose a figure? As far as I can determine, this tax has never been levied before in North America; it is a new tax.
I wish to state some reasons why the government is making another error by imposing this type of tax on newspapers. It may think it will just be applied to newspapers, but the tax will be paid by the people of this country, something the government seems to forget. The fact that the figure is raised from 75 to 80 per cent indicates that the members of the committee who raised Cain about it being 75 per cent were bought off by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for 5 per cent. The principle has not changed. The government simply raised it 5 per cent to keep its members quiet. It may have bought off its own members for 5 per cent, but it will not buy off the people of Canada for 5 per cent. Canadians will resent this tax.
We heard a considerable amount from the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), the hon. member for Broad-view-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) and others with regard to the
Excise Tax
effect on the dailies. I have the highest regard for the editor of the Edmonton Journal, Mr. O'Callaghan who was referred to a few moments ago. The statement was attributed to him that if someone wanted to have a catalogue included with a newspaper, it would be considered part of that press.
If it is only a case of trying to stop catalogues from being included as newspaper inserts, why not say that cannot be done? Why not do away with the catalogues? Why penalize everyone?
There are 18 or 20 weeklies in my constituency, some small some big. It is necessary for them to carry advertising. It is their only means of staying in business. Some are so small they are referred to as an advertising sheet. Many newspapers started out as an advertising sheet. I know of one that started as a one page advertising sheet with the odd bit of news. It was welcomed by the people. I have even seen sheets in restaurants which contain some news and very important advertising. It is a service to the people.
If the government is going to put these small weeklies out of business, there will be more bankruptcies.I do not know why the government is so intent on hurting small business. These weeklies carry the advertising for a week, in particular Saturday sales.
If we are not going to allow these inserts, the tax the newspapers will have to pay will be more than they are earning, or they will have to say to some people that they cannot accept their advertising. In what kind of position will that put our newspapers? They will be able to accept the advertising from one store but not another. The government is putting on a limit. The editor will be the scapegoat. He will have to decide what to accept and what not to accept. That is a questionable way of asking the newspapers to do business.
If this part of the bill passes, I hope that at the time of the next election the editors of these newspapers will not accept inserts from Liberal candidates because they voted in favour of this provision. That might teach them a lesson. The only way they learn is if it affects their pocketbook.
I have had newspaper inserts during an election. I felt they were valuable. Whether the people voted for or against me, they found out what I stood for and did not stand for. They were valuable to the newspapers because they were paid for them. Maybe I lost some votes, maybe I gained some, that is immaterial. The newspaper carried that information into every home in the area. It was a service to the community. Other candidates did the same. Often in the week or so before an election, inserts will be placed by three or four candidates.
The editor will be placed in the position of having to choose what to accept and what to reject. The reason is the newspapers will be taxed if it goes beyond the figure the minister pulled out of a hat, the figure that was increased to 80 per cent to buy off the Liberal members. The Liberals would not go for 75 per cent but they are quiet at 80 per cent.
Many of our newspapers are struggling. For many years the Canmore Miner was printed by a man who worked in the bosom of the earth. He printed the paper in his spare time.

June 10, 1981
Excise Tax
The mine is now closed and he is trying to make his living from printing the paper. It is a small paper and he needs the advertising and the inserts. The government wants to limit his advertising. It is a good paper and I hope he can stay in business, but that is questionable. Why hurt a small business which provides a service to the community only to provide another pound of flesh for the government? This is the first time such a tax has been levied on the newspapers of this country.
The Drumheller Mail is an excellent weekly. Sometimes it is very thick because there are so many advertising inserts. There are several stores in Drumheller. It is a large business area. The Mail is the only newspaper in that area. Everyone wants to advertise bargains for people shopping on Fridays and Saturdays. If the government proceeds in this way, these inserts will cost a lot of money. Every newspaper is going to experience the same difficulty. There are other newer newspapers, such as the Five Village Weekly at Irricana, which has just started up in the last two or three years. I believe it is doing all right. I do not know how it is doing financially, but I think it is keeping its head above water. Now we are going to make it difficult. That small paper will not be able to carry inserts. The same will be the case with the Nanton News, the Claresholm Local Press and several others I could mention. The percentage they will be taxed is an injustice to consumers as well because consumers have to know what the bargains are, and the newspapers will have to say they cannot carry this advertising because it will cost too much because of increased taxation. They may be put out of business, and consumers will be losers as well. The country will be the loser. When any business goes bankrupt, this country loses. It is a tragedy. This country loses whenever business goes bankrupt, and here we are laying out the cards for a number of our newspapers across the country to join the bankruptcy file which is building up. Consumers will lose because they will lose their opportunity of knowing what all the bargains are. They will not be able to go to the places where they can make their dollars go furthest.
When the minister spoke about taxes on liquor and tobacco, I did not hear one member on this side of the House say we are against taxes on liquor and tobacco. As a matter of fact, I have always said that those taxes are some of the better ones because people have a choice. They do not have to smoke, they do not have to chew and they do not have to drink. What we are saying is that we oppose the indexing of that tax. It is completely unfair. In addition, the government should remember that even in the tobacco business many people make their living by growing tobacco, packaging it and so forth.
Many farmers are earning good money from the malting of barley for beer. The same is the case with grapes used to make wine. These are Canadian industries, and we do not seem to look beyond our noses in relation to what this tax will do to the country, as the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) said a few moments ago.
This taxation will not stop the large dailies of Canada from publishing, but it may very well stop many of our small weeklies from going on. In order to stay in business they have to make profits, and this is just another expense which might well put a number of newspapers into bankruptcy. I wish government members would look at their own weekly newspapers and see what is happening before they are bought off for 5 per cent.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in what the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) was just saying because it again indicates that he has not read the provision. I do not think he really understands the nature of the amendment brought forward by the government to modify this provision.
As the minister indicated earlier, there are two different and separate provisions with respect to this tax. First, there is the tax as it would apply to newspapers. If, as the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) so correctly pointed out, a newspaper-let us call it a publication-is more than 90 per cent advertising, then it would be in a taxable category. If more than 50 per cent of the issues in any quarter are more than 80 per cent advertising, it would fall into a taxable category. When this was before the committee and then before the Senate committee, Les Hebdos du Quebec came before the Senate committee with the concern that their publications would be taxable, and the Senate committee looked at all the publications which were brought forward. I think ten different newspapers were brought forward. They were selected by Les Hebdos, and none of them would have been taxable under the previous 75 per cent rule, let alone the 80 per cent rule or 90 per cent rule we now propose. It is a red herring. It is highly unlikely that any of those small weekly newspapers will ever fall into a taxable category under this particular provision.
The other part of the tax deals with inserts. There is an important distinction to be made here because the creation of advertising-the printing of advertising-has always been taxable under the manufacturers' excise tax, which is what we are talking about here. It has always been taxable unless it has been distributed by newspapers.
One of the reasons this particular provision was brought forward-and the reason the tax change was considered in the first place-was that a number of independent distributors of advertising brochures are small companies. I heard the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) say he was in favour of small business and that we should look at the effects on small business. This tax change was considered in the first place precisely for that reason.
There were small businesses whose job it was and whose business it was to distribute house to house advertising flyers for other business firms. These business firms were being put into an unfair competitive position vis-a-vis newspapers because if anyone printed material and it was distributed by one of these small, independent distributors, the cost of printing and producing the advertising material was taxable under the manufacturers' excise tax. However, if the company doing
June 10, 1981

the advertising were to take that same thing down the street to a newspaper and have it included in the newspaper for distribution, it was not taxable.
If we are talking about tax equity, it seems to me that surely, if we are going to tax this material when it is distributed by one group of people, then either we should tax it when it is distributed by all groups of people or we should not tax it at all. That is a totally different argument, but what we said was that the tax as it was being applied was putting small business at a competitive disadvantage compared with large newspaper chains as well as with weekly newspapers, and that that should be rectified as there should be equity. So the correction was made. The fact of the matter was that many of the small companies which contacted us with regard to this inequity which was facing them as door to door distributors of material were forced out of business before this change could be made. There are still such companies in existence, but they will not be in existence much longer unless this change is brought forward. So we are talking about equity in the tax system.
The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood said the 80 per cent figure and the 90 per cent are arbitrary figures picked out of a hat, that they have no meaning but that the New Democratic Party has put forward a rational way of responding to this problem. "We are going to define a catalogue". What is a catalogue? Is it 20 pages, is it 10 pages, is it 8V6 by 11, is it 7 by 14 or is it 12 by 20? What is a catalogue? If the definition of a catalogue can be so objectively determined, then why does the hon. member accuse the government of being subjective in the definition of 80 per cent or 90 per cent, or in the definition of what shall, for the purposes of this tax, be a newspaper? That kind of inconsistency is typical of the New Democratic Party. Its definitions are objective; everyone else's are subjective. The concern of members of the New Democratic Party for a certain class of small business is fair and equitable, but our concern for small business is inequitable because we are not looking after the same class they happen to be looking after or at the same time.
The problem is, of course, they did not understand the rationale or logic for the change in the tax in the first place. We tried to explain it in committee but apparently we did not get across. The point is that this tax has been in place for a very long time. It is the manufacturers' excise tax, a tax which applies to printed material, and the question that was put to us was: if a newspaper expands into another field using its tax free status to make additional profits through the distribution system where it can be non-taxable, is that equitable to other non-newspaper firms which compete in the same field? We say, no. That is why we have brought forward the change, to retain equity in the tax system. The overwhelming evidence, Mr. Speaker, is that the weeklies will not be affected by this as a result of the 80-90 per cent definition. The inserts are taxable now in all places except when they are distributed by a newspaper, and we believe they should be taxed.

If the hon. members want to say all advertising should be tax free, that would be a proposal they could put forward. However, unless they are willing to do that, we say advertising that is printed and taxable in the hands of anybody should be taxable in the hands of everybody. That is equity, that is equality. That is what this party stands for, and that is what is in this particular amendment.

His colleague for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) raised a number of points concerning current distortions in the tax system. What I would like to stress is that he is indeed creating a new disparity, a new inequity, a new distortion by giving someone a tax break or rewarding someone who has to pay tax. Why not reward also the individual who has to file his income tax return? I submit that what he proposes to introduce in the tax system is basically wrong, because while supporting a proposal to create a tax burden, he says in the same breath: on the other hand, I will reward you for being a good Canadian citizen and paying your taxes. I submit his proposal is basically inconsistent. Second, it
would introduce inequity and perversion into the tax system. I therefore suggest he did not fully consider the repercussions of his amendment, because instead of helping one group of individuals or businesses, he would firstly introduce a flaw in our tax system and second he would thwart his colleague from Broadview-Greenwood who expressed the desire to see a tax system without distortion, inequity or inconsistencies.
Therefore, I prefer to support the views of his colleague from Broadview-Greenwood, of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and of members on this side of the House and reject such a proposal in order to maintain greater consistency within our tax system.
